# Results — Study 653 (Dividend-Cut-Drift)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — **"never
catch a falling dividend"**: a stock that cuts or omits its dividend keeps underperforming
afterward, because the board just told you, in the clearest language a board has, that the
outlook is worse than priced. The counter-claim: a dividend cut is backward-looking, the bad
news is already in the price by the ex-date, and the beaten-down "cutter" is a contrarian buy.
Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.
As-of **2026-06-30** (the last complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped).
Fingerprints `236c3c9bbc75` (SPY) / `06467e29de08` (event table).*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Universe | **101 named** large/mid-cap US "mature dividend payer" tickers (see [`dividend_cut_drift/data.py`](../dividend_cut_drift/data.py), `UNIVERSE`) — a deliberate mix of long-run stable payers and payers that visibly cut across four eras (2008-09 banks, 2015-16 energy, 2020 pandemic travel/retail, 2022-24 industrials/staples/apparel) |
| Loaded | **99/101** (2 skipped: `MRO`, `GPS` — both renamed/delisted post-acquisition, not fetchable from yfinance as of 2026-06) |
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (total-return) closes per ticker + SPY (7,673 rows, 1996-01-02 → 2026-06-30), and yfinance's raw per-ticker `Dividends`/`Stock Splits` streams |
| Event detection | **cut** = a scheduled payment ≤ 70% of the prior payment; **omission** = a gap ≥ 1.8× the ticker's own trailing typical interval (payers with no regular sub-200-day cadence excluded). Both computed on a **split-adjusted** dividend stream with one-off special-dividend/spinoff/stub artifacts stripped (documented heuristic — see `strategy.strip_special_dividends`); a 4-payment warm-up excludes a freshly-initiated payer's irregular early specials from being read as "cuts" |
| Events | **173 detected** (108 cuts, 65 omissions) across **64 of 99** tickers, 1997-02-05 → 2026-02-13; **172** have a full [−20, +120]-trading-day window on the tape by as-of (1 too recent) |
| Execution / costs | **one documented convention**: the cut/omission is only knowable from the close of the event day (the ex-date on which the payment record shows it); trades enter the **next session's close** (day +1) and exit 120 trading days later; round trip = 2 × one-way cost × NAV; shorts additionally pay a flat 50 bps/yr borrow, accrued over the holding period |
| Statistics | cross-sectional one-sample *t* on each event's CAR (primary); Newey-West(5) *t* on the daily equal-weight "cutters" calendar-time portfolio (overlap-robust cross-check — events share calendar time, so the cross-sectional test's independence assumption is imperfect); Wilson interval on the hit rate; 20-seed × 200-draw random ticker/date placebo |
| Survivorship — **named on the Signal axis** | every name in the universe is a **current survivor** (still listed as of 2026). Names that cut a dividend and later went bankrupt or were delisted outright (Lehman Brothers, Washington Mutual, pre-2009 GM, Eastman Kodak, Circuit City, RadioShack, Bear Stearns…) are, by construction, absent. This almost certainly biases every drift estimate below **upward** (less negative than the true population effect) — the worst outcomes of "catching a falling dividend" are structurally excluded from a survivor-only basket |

## The headline — cross-sectional CAR (ticker log return − SPY log return)

| horizon | mean CAR | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| pre-event [−20..−1] | **+0.75%** | +0.59 |
| post-event [+1..+20] | −0.59% | −0.52 |
| post-event [+1..+60] | −0.57% | −0.29 |
| **post-event [+1..+120]** | **−0.31%** | **−0.14** |

n = 172 events. Hit rate (CAR[+1..+120] < 0, i.e. "kept falling"): **82/172 = 47.7%**
(Wilson 95% [40.3%, 55.1%]) — statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip.

**No pre-event drift, either.** The market shows no measurable anticipation of the cut in the
20 sessions before it (*t* = +0.59) — consistent with the event date (the ex-date on which the
payment record first shows the cut) not lagging the market's own information by much, at least
not in a way this window catches.

**Cut vs omission — same test, split by type:**

| type | n | mean CAR[+1..+120] | *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| cut (partial reduction) | 107 | −3.61% | −1.25 |
| omission (full stop) | 65 | **+5.13%** | +1.55 |

An intriguing but **uncertified** split: partial cuts point (mildly) toward continued
underperformance, full omissions point (mildly) toward a bounce — plausibly a "kitchen sink"
capitulation read — but neither individually nor combined clears *t* = 2.

## Calendar-time cross-check — Newey-West on the daily portfolio

| metric | value |
|---|--:|
| portfolio-days | 6,123 |
| mean daily abnormal return | −3.28 bps |
| Newey-West(5) *t* | **−1.23** |

The overlap-robust check (events share calendar time; the cross-sectional test above treats them
as independent draws, which they are not) agrees with the cross-sectional result: **no
significant drift**.

## Daily-level Welch cross-check

A third, differently-shaped cut on the same question: pool every ticker-day abnormal return
inside a post-event window ("treatment") against every other day for the same tickers
("control"), then a two-sample Welch *t* on the pooled daily distributions.

| group | n | mean daily AR |
|---|--:|--:|
| treatment (post-event window) | 20,100 | −0.79 bps |
| control (same tickers, other days) | 438,031 | −1.18 bps |
| Welch *t* | | **+0.16** |

A third method, a third non-result — cross-sectional, calendar-time NW and pooled-daily Welch
all agree.

## Random-date placebo

20 seeds × 200 draws (4,000 total) of 172 random ticker/date pairs, mean post-120 CAR:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| observed mean CAR[+1..+120] | −0.31% |
| placebo mean (sd) | −1.04% (1.60%) |
| *p*-value (left tail: is the observed more negative than a random calendar?) | **0.675** |

The observed drift is **less** negative than a typical random 172-event draw — the opposite of
what "never catch a falling dividend" predicts. This is not evidence *for* a positive effect
either (the placebo mean itself reflects nothing but the average idiosyncratic drag of individual
stocks over a 140-session window vs SPY); it simply confirms the observed mean is unremarkable.

## Third axis — two tradable expressions, one execution lag

Enter the close the session **after** the event day (the cut/omission is only knowable from that
close — zero look-ahead), exit 120 trading days later. Costs = 2 × one-way × NAV; shorts also pay
50 bps/yr borrow. "Excess" = net return minus the return of the **matched-exposure benchmark**
over the identical window (long SPY for the long leg; short SPY for the short leg — the natural
zero-information comparison for a directional position).

| side | cost | net/event | *t* (net) | excess/event | *t* (excess) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| short-the-cutter | 5 bps | **−15.18%** | −3.98 | −6.27% | −1.86 |
| short-the-cutter | 10 bps | −15.28% | −4.00 | −6.37% | −1.89 |
| buy-the-cutter (timer) | 5 bps | **+14.74%** | +3.86 | +5.83% | +1.73 |
| buy-the-cutter (timer) | 10 bps | +14.64% | +3.83 | +5.73% | +1.70 |

| side | hit rate (net>0) | worst event | best event | Sharpe(net) | Sharpe(excess) | events/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| short-the-cutter | 41.9% [34.7%, 49.3%] | **−467.4%** | +79.0% | −0.74 | −0.35 | 5.9 |
| buy-the-cutter | 57.6% [50.1%, 64.7%] | −79.4% | **+467.0%** | +0.72 | +0.32 | 5.9 |

The **net** (gross-of-market-beta) numbers look dramatic in both directions — but that's almost
entirely the 120-trading-day (~6 month) holding period riding the market's own drift, not a
cutter-specific effect: strip it out (the "excess" column, matched-exposure) and **neither leg
clears the certification bar** (short *t* = −1.86, long *t* = +1.73 — both close, neither over
2). Short-the-cutter additionally carries genuine squeeze tail risk: one event alone (a naked
short caught in a recovery rally) lost **−467%** of the position — a single bad trade that no
position-sizing discipline survives undiluted.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic single-factor market-model panel with a scheduled planted "cut" event and a
TUNABLE post-event abnormal drift; no network.

| world | mean post-120 CAR | *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (drift = 0), **20 seeds** | — | mean **−0.15** (sd 1.14), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 1/20 seeds** |
| planted drift = −0.001/day (seed 653, n=89) | **−9.35%** | **−3.84** |

The null fires at essentially the nominal ~5% false-positive rate of a *t* = 2 threshold (1/20,
not a systematic bias), and a planted drift lights up cleanly. *(A faithful-engine / power check
only — never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The academic anchor (Michaely, Thaler & Womack 1995; Boehme & Sorescu 2002)
  documents a genuine multi-year post-omission drift on 1960s-90s NYSE/AMEX data. On **this**
  real tape — 172 events, 1997-2025, a survivor-biased modern large-cap basket, a 120-trading-day
  (~6 month) window — the drift is statistically nothing: cross-sectional *t* = −0.14, Newey-West
  *t* = −1.23, placebo *p* = 0.68, hit rate 47.7% (a coin flip). Decades of published support plus
  a sub-2 *t* on our sample is the textbook `WEAK` case, not `REAL`.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Neither short-the-cutter (*t* = −1.86) nor buy-the-cutter
  (*t* = +1.73) clears *t* ≥ 2 net of costs, matched for market exposure. The gross numbers that
  *do* look dramatic (−15% short, +15% long, per event) are riding six months of ordinary market
  beta, not a cutter-specific edge — and the short leg carries a documented −467% single-event
  tail.
- **"Does the falling dividend keep falling?" — BUSTED.** Not supported on the modern real tape:
  the point estimate is a near-zero wash (post-120 CAR −0.31%, *t* = −0.14), the hit rate is a
  coin flip, and the two event subtypes even point in **opposite**, individually-uncertified
  directions (cuts mildly negative, omissions mildly positive). The folklore's mechanism — cuts
  as a credible bad-news signal the market underreacts to — may have been real once; it doesn't
  replicate here.
